warnings.warning: Physical page 1 has no text layer; its Summary was visually transcribed and must not be treated as machine-extracted text coverage.

The abstract says Priority covers 80 percent and Bone Growth about 50 percent, while the memo compresses the range to 70 to 50 percent and the Y=225 table implies about 83.45 percent occupancy for Priority.
The abstract calls the solution nearly optimal without a global optimum, bound, or comparator against exact small instances.
The introduction says a failed naive trip is discarded, while the algorithm removes its trip length from the distribution after all launch nights fail; those are different rejection semantics.
The paper alternates among trip days, rafting days, nights, stops, six-to-eighteen, and seven-to-nineteen without one explicit indexing convention.
S1 uses campsite values through Y+1 while S2 uses campsite rows and trip identifiers through X, but the conversion, launch, exit, and zero conventions are not formalized.

Open Campsite percent is described as an unoccupied fraction but then said never to reach 100 percent for boundary reasons; the denominator and whether launch/exit cells count require a typed definition.
C(Y)=max X(Y)/Y depends on an unstated feasible-set maximum, target distribution, horizon, and crossover policy, so carrying capacity changes meaning across models.
Craft choice is postponed until after scheduling even though some short trips require daily distance beyond the assumed oar maximum.
The guaranteed-distance discussion derives 64 motor miles but later uses 32 oar miles without the same explicit derivation and ignores weather, flow, stops, and within-day congestion.
The campsite-spacing histogram lacks visible sample size, bin specification, source-cleaning procedure, uncertainty, and a direct mapping from the two source rivers to the synthetic river.
Unlimited launch equipment, labor, dock, and arrival capacity can create extreme daily clusters that the objective never penalizes.
Night-only discretization permits arbitrary within-day crossovers and congestion, then treats crossover penalties as a partial repair rather than testing travel feasibility.
The scheduling-theory comparison is qualitative and does not establish that integer programming or alternative network formulations are computationally infeasible.
The naive nearest-available rule does not define tolerance, tie-breaking probability, daily reach boundaries, or rollback after a later night fails.
Priority uses a probability-p sort-or-shuffle step, but no seed, repeated-run protocol, or uncertainty interval is supplied.
Ranking camps primarily by whether they incur a crossover is underspecified when multiple existing trips and order relations are present.
Priority removes trips that cannot be assigned on a night but does not backtrack to reuse space that those trips occupied on earlier nights.
The density model declares all trips equally important but still has to choose signs randomly at identical positions and choose which trip to discard in an unresolved collision.
Equation (1) is explicitly limited to nonzero separation within one campsite distance; exact ties are described by random mapping to plus or minus one outside the displayed formula.
Repeatedly subtracting density has no step size, stop tolerance, maximum iteration count, convergence proof, or test for oscillation and boundary violations.
A one-to-one campsite mapping is asserted for certain near-spacing patterns without a specified matching algorithm or proof for the full set of boats.
Figure 4 reports 1978 trips for Density Perturbation, while the main table reports 1811 for D.Pertb.; scenario or implementation differences are not reconciled.
Bone Heuristic 1 is presented as determining an optimal alternating sequence without proof that other no-crossover launch orders cannot dominate it.
Center squeezing is called a necessary condition but the travel-speed, campsite, launch, and finish constraints used in its feasibility test are not fully formalized.
The greedy score used to select the best inserted trip is not defined mathematically, and no tie rule or complexity analysis is given.
Bone Growth guarantees no crossovers for its constructed schedule but only claims a local optimum and is highly sensitive to the initial bone.
The motor-oar extension is incomplete because the spreading algorithm was not adjusted for the lower flexibility of oar craft.
The final table header is visually ambiguous as 'Var from Distr -10^4'; its scaling must be preserved as uncertain rather than silently read as multiplication or division.
The Density Perturbation row uses Y=200 while the other main comparisons use 45, 150, and 225, preventing a like-for-like ranking.
Bones2 produces more trips largely because it contains shorter trips and substantially misses the stated target distribution, so throughput and distribution fidelity cannot be merged.
Removing high-crossover trips reduced campsite coverage by 10 to 15 percent but no scenario, repeat count, or uncertainty is reported.
Priority crossover growth is described as exponential from three campsite settings without a fitted model, residuals, or broader scale sweep.
The conclusion converts roughly 29 crossovers per trip into less than one contact per hour without defining whether crossover count equals passenger contact or how trip duration enters.
The memo reports carrying capacity 12.5 to 7.5 and omits the approximately 9 trips-per-campsite Bones2 result stated in the body.
The memo says both algorithms can generate any desired trip ratio, while the results show persistent short-trip skew and especially poor Bones2 distribution matching.

global_organization_chain: Summary chain: decision and three objectives -> Priority, Density, and Bone mechanisms -> occupancy and crossover results -> distribution and robustness -> preference-conditioned recommendation.
Abstract chain: model definitions -> shared occupancy objective -> quantified Priority/Bone tradeoff -> scaling and sensitivity -> launch-time regularity -> nearly-optimal claim.
Introduction chain: river and craft facts -> campsite and wildlife constraints -> scheduling difficulty -> standard-method gap -> four-model ladder.
Notation chain: operational terms -> two schedule matrices -> occupancy metric -> travel guarantee -> multi-objective problem -> carrying capacity.
Assumption chain: craft-length correlation -> no hybrid trips -> daily reach -> campsite evidence -> unlimited launches -> night-only state.
Problem-analysis chain: ordered river jobs -> unique sections -> mismatch with identical-machine scheduling -> unit campsite queue and balking.
Naive chain: empty schedule -> sampled trip -> launch-night search -> nearest open camps -> failure removal -> blocking and crossover diagnosis.
Priority chain: remaining-distance urgency -> nightly cooperation -> optional randomization -> preferred camp -> crossover-aware fallback -> completed or active state.
Density motivation chain: shortest-trip priority critique -> continuous equal-distance target -> local crowding -> signed density -> iteration -> discrete mapping.
Bone chain: no-crossover objective -> alternating launch heuristic -> center-packing heuristic -> greedy insertion -> saturation -> temporal spreading.
Testing chain: ordered criteria -> campsite and target scenarios -> four metrics -> comparison table -> model-specific trends.
Priority-results chain: more sites -> more trips and variety -> carrying-capacity figures -> crossover growth -> dense schedule visual.
Bone-results chain: two starting bones -> saturation with short trips -> symmetry -> throughput/distribution tradeoff -> capacity figures.
Analysis chain: trips -> distribution -> open sites -> crossovers -> carrying capacity -> removal experiment -> temporal consistency.
Strength-limitation chain: model benefit -> mechanism -> failure mode -> parameter sensitivity -> proposed repair.
Conclusion chain: accept passing -> choose Priority; forbid passing -> choose Bone; seek middle ground -> mix; improve initialization and optimization.
Memo chain: management objective -> two algorithms -> capacity range -> schedule deliverables -> assumptions -> model choice -> mixed pricing option.
The final warning pass reconciles OCR, formula, indexing, algorithm, convergence, scenario, table, metric, claim, and memo conflicts without replacing positive learning.
